look_here_first: INTRODUCED annual bluegrass: soft low light-green grass in lawns and paths with small open pale green panicles; folded emerging blades with boat-prow tips and a translucent short membranous ligule. Usually annual, though persistent biotypes occur. True flowers are generally bisexual, unlike dioecious Texas bluegrass.

best_field_traits: Cool-season generally annual; persistent biotypes can occur in managed moist turf.
Low flowering tuft with small spreading greenish seedheads; can flower under close mowing.
Young folded blades have prow-like boat-shaped tips; this is a genus clue NOT species-specific.
Ligule membranous around 0.5–3 mm according to Williamson County treatment; no auricles.
Spikelets commonly with bisexual florets; unlike separate-sex Texas bluegrass.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Boat-shaped leaf tip and true collar membrane at calibrated close distance
Entire rooted tuft including roots and potential spreading basal nodes
Spikelet with fertile florets, glumes and fine basal hairs under magnification
crew_field_check: Inspect actual rooted base, not only head silhouette.
Boat-shaped leaf tip is shared by Poa species.
Photograph true membranous ligule and mature spikelet/floret details.
Never count Texas bluegrass webby hairs from a blurred landscape view.

comparisons.key_distinctions: P. arachnifera is a rhizomatous native perennial, often taller in spring prairie/open-oak habitat, with separate male and female plants. Female heads can appear cobwebby because of dense fine hairs at lemma bases. P. annua is typically a small introduced flowering tuft whose flowerheads are pale green and have bisexual florets. Both have boat tips, so inspect whole root system and florets.
